title: The icon wars
hook: emperors smashed icons; John of Damascus argued that since God became visible, he can be painted

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hagia Sophia, and your line was a dome of light. Did you find a high ceiling and look straight up? Today we stay in the same city, and the walls of its churches. Day eight hundred one.

Workmen climb a ladder outside a palace gate in Constantinople. Above the gate hangs an image of Christ. They've been sent to take it down. Tradition says a crowd of ordinary people gathered at the foot of the ladder, and some of them were women, and they shook it until the man on it fell. Whether every detail happened that way or not, the story shows what was at stake. For a long stretch, on and off, Christians in the eastern empire fought over pictures: whether a church could hold an image of Christ, of Mary, of the saints, or whether those images had to go. Today's word is the name for breaking them.
screen: `A CROWD AT THE FOOT OF IT.`

segments.voice: Iconoclasm means image-breaking, and an iconoclast is an image-breaker. Today we use the word for anyone who smashes a tradition. Here it meant it literally. Some emperors ordered icons removed, plastered over, or destroyed, and people who defended them were punished. It's easy to make the iconoclasts the villains. Be fair to them. Their argument came straight from scripture. The commandment, in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." They worried that Christians were bowing to wood and paint, and that God, who has no body, can't be pictured at all. That was a serious worry, held by believers. Then a monk named John, born in Damascus and living in a monastery near Jerusalem, outside the emperor's reach, wrote back. His answer turns on one idea. In the old days, he said in effect, God had no body and no face, so no one could make an image of him. But now God has been seen. The Word became flesh. He walked, ate, wept, was touched. So I paint what I have seen. I don't worship the wood, he said; I worship the maker of matter, who became matter for my sake. Paul's letter to the Colossians gives him his key phrase. Christ, in the King James words, is "the image of the invisible God." If God has already made an image of himself, a human face, then a picture of that face isn't an insult to the invisible God. It's a way of saying he really came. Christians still differ here. Orthodox and Catholic Christians use icons and images in prayer. Some Protestant churches have pictures and crosses; some keep their walls deliberately plain, out of the same care for the commandment. Each side is trying to honor the same God.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT MAKE ANY GRAVEN IMAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an image of Christ. Any one: an icon, a painting, a stained-glass window, a small picture in a book, or one you find on your phone. Settle, and breathe. Look at the face. Notice who made it, roughly where, how they imagined him. Notice the eyes. If you pray, you can let the image be a window rather than the point, and pray through it. If you don't, simply look, and notice that someone, somewhere, painted this because they believed a face had been seen. The bell holds the time.
Iconoclasm. Image-breaking: the struggle in the eastern church over whether Christ and the saints could be pictured, and the name for smashing images.
Your line: the invisible became visible. Today, notice one face that shows you something you can't see directly: kindness, grief, patience. Day eight hundred one.

howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians pray with icons and images, often lighting a candle or kissing an icon; some Protestant churches keep images and crosses, and others keep their walls plain out of care for the commandment against graven images.

fork.setup: you're John of Damascus. the emperor says pictures of Christ break the commandment. how do you answer?
options: God has now been seen in Christ, so I can paint what I've seen.
pictures are just decoration, so it doesn't matter.
fork.reveal: John's case rests on the incarnation: the invisible God became visible, so his human face can be painted.

original.note: Greek: image, the word in "the image of the invisible God."

trapdoor: what you thought: an iconoclast is someone who breaks the rules.
what it means: literally an image-breaker. Christians fought over whether Christ and the saints could be pictured.
what a scholar hears: two scriptural arguments: no graven image, and the image of the invisible God made flesh.

notes: Hook: the removal of the Christ icon at the Chalke Gate and the women who shook the ladder is attributed to tradition (later hagiographic sources); confirm wording.
The hook says the struggle lasted 'for generations, on and off' (usually dated c. 726–787 and 814–843); no numbers stated per the claims rule. Confirm.
'Iconoclasm means image-breaking': a definition (Greek eikon + klao); confirm.

John of Damascus, On the Divine Images 1.16 (and 1.4, 1.8): 'I do not worship matter, I worship the Creator of matter who became matter for my sake'. Paraphrased as reported speech, not quoted; confirm.
Emperors are not named (Leo III, Constantine V). Confirm.
The description of the iconoclasts' case (fear of idolatry; God without body cannot be depicted) is meant to be fair; a Keeper should confirm.
Protestant practice described as varied, without ranking; confirm.
Editor pass: 'for generations' (an implied span) became 'for a long stretch'; trimmed the repeated 'serious... serious' line.

Audit 3: corrected 'a monk named John, living in Damascus': John was from Damascus but wrote his defenses of icons as a monk near Jerusalem (Mar Saba), under Muslim rule and outside the emperor's reach; confirm. Hook: in the Chalke Gate tradition one official on the ladder fell, so 'the workmen fell' became 'the man on it fell'.
